title: Understanding MVC Architecture
description: Learn the Model-View-Controller (MVC) architectural pattern, how it separates concerns in web applications, and why this separation makes your code easier to maintain, test, and scale.

blocks.text: The **Model-View-Controller (MVC)** pattern is an architectural design pattern that separates an application into three interconnected components. Each component has a distinct responsibility, which makes the application easier to develop, test, and maintain.

In ASP.NET Core, MVC is not just a pattern you follow — it is a first-class framework feature. The framework provides controllers, views, model binding, and routing that all work together to implement the MVC pattern seamlessly.
Understanding what each component does and how they communicate is the foundation of everything else you will learn in this course.

blocks.title: Model — the data and business logic
items: Represents the shape and rules of your application data
Contains C# classes (POCOs — Plain Old CLR Objects) with properties
May include validation rules and business logic
Has no knowledge of how data is displayed or how requests arrive
Examples: `Product`, `Order`, `Customer` classes

blocks.title: View — the user interface
items: Generates the HTML that the browser displays
Written in Razor syntax, which mixes HTML and C# code
Receives a model from the controller and renders it
Should contain minimal logic — mostly display logic
Examples: `Index.cshtml`, `Details.cshtml`, `_Layout.cshtml`

blocks.title: Controller — the request handler
items: Receives incoming HTTP requests from the user's browser
Contains action methods, each handling a specific request
Interacts with models (and services/repositories) to get or update data
Selects a view to render and passes the model to it
Examples: `HomeController`, `ProductsController`, `AccountController`

blocks.text: How MVC Works Together: A Request Flow
When a user visits a page, the following sequence of events occurs. Understanding this flow will help you know where to add code for each type of task.

blocks.title: The MVC request lifecycle
items: The user types a URL like `/products/details/5` into their browser
The **routing system** matches the URL to a controller action — `ProductsController.Details(5)`
The **controller action** receives the request, extracts the route data (id = 5), and fetches the product from a repository
The controller creates a model object (the Product) and passes it to a **view**
The **view** receives the model, reads its properties, and generates HTML
The HTML response is sent back to the browser, and the user sees the product details page

blocks.title: Separation of concerns in practice
blocks.text: Notice how each layer only knows about its neighbors. The view does not know where the product data came from, and the controller does not know how the view renders HTML. This loose coupling means you can change the view's HTML without touching the controller, or swap the data source without rewriting any views.
Let us look at a concrete example with a simple product catalog. The `Product` class is the model, `ProductsController` is the controller, and `Details.cshtml` is the view.

blocks.title: The Model — Product class
blocks.content: A simple C# class representing a product. This is the data shape shared across the application.

blocks.title: The Controller — ProductsController
blocks.content: The controller receives the request, gets data from a source, and passes it to a view.

blocks.title: The View — Details.cshtml
blocks.content: The Razor view receives the Product model and renders it as HTML.

blocks.text: In this example: the **Model** (`Product`) is a plain C# class. The **Controller** (`ProductsController`) receives the HTTP request, looks up the product by ID, and calls `return View(product)`. The **View** (`Details.cshtml`) uses `@Model` to access the product's properties and render them as HTML.

Without separation of concerns, web applications quickly become difficult to manage. Imagine a single file containing database queries, HTML markup, and HTTP request handling — updating any part would risk breaking everything else.

blocks.title: Benefits of the MVC pattern
items: **Easier maintenance** — Each component has one job. Changes are localized and predictable
**Parallel development** — A frontend developer can work on views while a backend developer works on controllers and models
**Testability** — Models and controllers can be unit-tested independently of the UI
**Reusability** — The same model and controller logic can serve multiple views (HTML page, JSON API, PDF export)
**Clear organization** — New developers can quickly understand the project structure

blocks.title: Views should be thin
blocks.text: A common mistake is putting business logic inside views. Views should only display data — any logic (calculations, data filtering, decisions) belongs in the model or controller. Keeping views thin makes them easier to redesign and test.

Most modern web frameworks implement some form of MVC or a variation of it. Django (Python), Ruby on Rails, Laravel (PHP), and Spring MVC (Java) all follow the same core principle of separating data, presentation, and request handling.

terms.definition: The data structure and business logic of the application. In ASP.NET Core, models are plain C# classes (POCOs) with properties representing data.
The user interface component. Razor views (.cshtml files) combine HTML markup with embedded C# code to render dynamic pages.
The request handler. Controller classes contain action methods that receive HTTP requests, process them, and return responses (often via views).
A design principle where each part of the application has a distinct responsibility. MVC enforces separation by isolating data, UI, and request handling.
Plain Old CLR Object — a simple C# class without dependencies on specific frameworks. Models are typically POCOs for maximum flexibility and testability.

blocks.title: Trace an MVC Request Through the Codebase
blocks.description: Use your MVC project to trace a full request from URL to rendered HTML, identifying the model, controller, and view at each step.
steps: In your MyFirstApp project, open the Controllers folder and find HomeController.cs
Open the `Index()` action method and note what it returns — does it return a view?
Navigate to the Views/Home folder and find Index.cshtml — this is the view rendered by the Index action
At the top of Index.cshtml, note the `@model` directive — this declares what model type the view expects

Add a `ViewBag.Message = "Hello from MVC!"` line to the Index action, then add `

@ViewBag.Message

` to the view
Run the app and confirm the message appears on the home page
blocks.expectedOutcome: You can explain which controller action handles the home page request, how the view receives data from the controller, and how `ViewBag` provides an additional data channel from controller to view.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: MVC separates an application into Model (data), View (UI), and Controller (request handler)
The controller receives the request, interacts with models, and selects a view
Views use Razor syntax to mix HTML and C# code for dynamic rendering
Models are plain C# classes (POCOs) representing your application data
Separation of concerns makes code easier to maintain, test, and extend
The request flows: URL → Router → Controller → Model → View → HTML response
blocks.takeaway: MVC is the organizational backbone of ASP.NET Core. Understanding the three components and how they communicate is the key to building well-structured web applications that are easy to maintain and scale.
